title: The Name Rides
blurb: Ila signs her own name to a stranger's knot, and the slack that falls lands on her father's workbench, while a dead man pours her tea.

blocks.text: I kneel in wet soil with a borrowed fid in one hand and a docket in the other, and I sign my own name on the keeper's line while Orla Treadgold watches and does not help.

Item: two strands, one garden cobble, inside my reach. Item: I have no licence, so this is a crime, and I am doing it anyway. Item: whatever it sends me, it lands on me and nobody else. Item: Dad never has to know.
I tie the docket's tag to the fid. Orla's fid has no number stamped on its collar. Over on the potting bench the coin is still standing on its edge.
"Whenever you're ready, Clerk," says Orla. "Or not."

I lifted the cobble out of its row along the path myself, and now it sits in the hollow I pressed for it in the bed, brown and smooth, the size of a big potato. I swing it one more time to be sure. The bob goes crooked, circles twice, and settles. Two. No hesitation before the count. No half-turn. I checked that three times before I signed, because the last time I untied a two, a man's heart stopped.
I put the point of the fid in.

It feels nothing like the frames in the Registry basement. Here the knot runs through the stone and the starlings on the fence and the drip off the shed roof, and the fid finds the first strand the way your foot finds a stair in the dark. A minute a strand, and nobody interrupts. Orla doesn't even breathe loudly. I ease the first strand out, then the second, and the cobble goes quiet under my hand.
That's all. A brown stone in wet soil. When I swing it now, the bob falls still and straight.
"Two minutes," says Orla. "Then it's off my bed and on its way to you."

The dwell. I stand next to my own bad luck while it makes up its mind, which is the longest two minutes I have ever stood anywhere. Then the minutes are over, and somewhere in the next twenty-four hours, two strands are coming for me.
"Those two are relaxed now," says Orla, and takes her fid back and wipes it on her jacket. "A year and a day. Nobody ties them. Nobody catches them."
"And not me," I say. "A keeper isn't a strand of the knot. I'm just where it lands."
"Listen to her." She is already kneeling at the next bed. "Come back when it's fallen. Not before. I don't teach people who are waiting for something."
At twenty to eight the next morning I'm at our front gate in my work coat with my packed lunch, waiting for the post.

Slack falls against the grain of what you truly want. I learned that on my knees, with every page from my drawer spilled round me. So I know what my two strands will aim at. There is a letter from Standards on its way, and there is a man in our kitchen who thinks I file insurance claims on Quay Street.
Gareth the postman comes round the corner at quarter to, like always.
"Morning, Gareth! Anything for forty-one?"
"Not today, Ila." He fans the bundle at me. "Gas bill for fourteen, catalogue for the Pruetts. That's your lot."
"Thank you, Gareth! Have a lovely round."
Nothing for us. I wave him all the way to the corner. On the 8:10 Wilf says, "Morning, Bureau," and I say, "Morning, Wilf!" and ride to Tallow Row like I do every morning now.

Dorrie's café is opposite the Bureau's front steps. I have the window table and a pot of tea, and I can see Stan through the glass doors across the road. At half past eight a woman comes in out of the rain, looks at every table in the place, and sits down at mine without asking.
She's fifty or so, in a donkey jacket with a union badge on the lapel, and she puts a sheaf of typed pages down between us. Every line on them is a complaint from my drawer.

"Ila Brandt," she says. It isn't a question. "Magdalena Danquah. Shop steward, Amalgamated Society of Docket Porters. Your man on the desk says you sit in here every morning like a dog outside a butcher's."
"That's Stan. He's lovely. Hello! Would you like some tea? Dorrie does a—"
"I'm not here for tea."
My heart goes quick. Here it is, I think. She's my two strands. She must be, and she knows everything.

"Under the agreement," says Mags, "where Management takes up any paper bearing the name of a member, the Society shall have sight thereof. So Standards sent us this." She taps the pages. "Your drawer. Two hundred and twelve complaints Management stamped No Action. Eleven of them name my members as keepers."
"I copied them because they cluster. By address. Nobody would—"

"I know why you copied them. You're the only one in that building who looked twice." She doesn't say it like a compliment. "So I'll tell you what I've got, and you'll tell me what Management means to do about it."

She lays three names down, one at a time, like cards. "Joyce Mallender. Kit Farrow. Dennis Abara. Members in good standing. Each one signed for a clearance this past week, routine work, and took their fall same as always. That's the trade."
"So what happened?"

"A woman turns up on Joyce's doorstep with her arm in a sling. A van door knocked her off her bike on Quay Street, and as she lay in the road, a phone on the pavement said, clear as you like, 'Joyce Mallender.' A roofer's ladder goes, and somebody across the yard shouts 'Kit Farrow.' A pallet comes down on a fishwife's foot at the market, and the tannoy pages Dennis Abara."
"How did they find them?"

"Looked the names up. Then they knocked on my members' doors and asked them what they'd done." Mags lays her palm flat on the table. "The Society's rule, and it's older than you are: no member shall be made to bear any fall but that which he has signed for in his own hand. My members never signed for a woman in a sling."
I've been hearing that ambulance radio for nine days. I'm not good at keeping things in.
"Somebody heard my name too," I say. "On an ambulance radio. A man on the Lantry Steps."
Mags looks at me properly for the first time. "Did he get hurt?"
"No. He got saved."
"Then it isn't the same thing, is it."
"It might be! It might be the same thing the other way up, and I want to help, I really do, I'll write it all up, I'll take it to—"
"To who? You're suspended."
"I'm... yes."

"Suspended is still Management. It's just Management with time on its hands." She stands and buttons her jacket. "I don't need help, Miss Brandt. I've had Management's help for twenty years. I need somebody in that building made to answer. When you find out who, you come and find me. The hall's on Cable Street."
She takes her pages and goes, and my tea goes cold in front of me. She wasn't my two strands. So they're still out there, and I don't know where.
At ten to twelve I take Dad his lunch, because the twenty-four hours are nearly up and nothing has happened, and I have started to hope the slack got lost.

The lock-up door is rolled half up. The radio's on low. Dad has a wheel clamped between his knees and the spoke key in his right hand, and on the workbench beside him, propped against a tin of grease, is a long brown envelope with the Bureau crest in the corner.
I know that envelope before I can read it. Four years of my life went out in envelopes like it.
Through the little window on the front it says: STANDARDS. NOTICE TO SUSPENDED OFFICER. CLERK I. BRANDT. And our address, with the four and the one both perfectly clear.
"Came for you," says Dad. He doesn't look up. "Pruett boy brought it. Gareth took it to fourteen first."

Mrs Pruett must have given it to her Dylan to bring round. Dylan passes this door on his way to school, with our name painted on it, so he left it here. Gareth on his round. Dylan on his way to school. Two strands, and neither of them meant a thing by it.
The envelope hasn't been opened. Dad has never opened a letter of mine in his life.
"Dad—"
"The Bureau," he says. Very quietly. He spins the wheel and watches it run. "How long?"
"Four years."
"Four years." He nods, the same slow nod he gave my missing pass. "And suspended."
"Eight days."
He puts the spoke key down. When he looks at me it's worse than if he'd shouted. "Is it me? Did they find out about me?"
He knows the conflict rule. Of course he knows it. He was a Porter.
"No," I say. "No, Dad. It isn't you. They don't know about you. It's something else, it's paper, it's—"
"Good." That's all. Good. He doesn't ask what the something else is. He picks the wheel back up. "This hub's had it. I'll want a new one from the wholesaler."
"I'm sorry," I say. "I'm sorry I lied to you."
"Your lunch is going cold, Inspector."
It's cheese sandwiches. I nearly laugh, because if he's teasing me, he's still talking to me.
The rule held. The keeper takes the slack and nobody else: my letter, my lie, my two strands. And it's my father sitting there, turning a wheel that doesn't need turning.
The rain has stopped by the time I climb the terrace steps at Nettlecombe. The third step still rocks. Orla is kneeling in the bed beside Pilchard, and she doesn't look round.
"It fell, then."
"On my dad's workbench."
"On you."
"On me," I say. "Through him."

She nods, as if that's the right answer and she's sorry it is. I sit on the edge of the path and tell her all of it: three Porters, three strangers hurt, three names out of a phone and a shout and a tannoy, and one name out of an ambulance radio. When I get to the Porters, her trowel stops. Just for a second. Then it goes on.
"Why would anyone hear a name inside an accident?" I ask. "It's not in the book. Slack falls on the keeper, one coincidence of equal weight. It doesn't go to strangers and it doesn't carry names."
"Not when it's left alone," says Orla. "What can you do with slack in the dwell?"
"Catch it. Tie it into a knot of your own. That's in the book."
"Now tie the catch first. Before the knot's ever untied." She turns the soil over. "Leave it waiting at the anchor. With a design, and a person to go to."
"And when the knot comes undone?"
"The slack goes to that person. Shaped. And the keeper's full name goes with it. On a radio. Out of a stranger's mouth." She is quiet a long moment. "The name rides."
"Bureau doctrine says slack can't be shaped."
"Bureau doctrine says the Lantry Steps was a man with a weak heart." She pulls a weed. "Never mind strangers. Your steps. You untied the outer knot. What does a slip inside do?"
"Lets go."
"And its slack goes on the docket of the untie that let it go. All of it, with the outer, as one fall. Never on whoever tied the slip. Not one strand."
"I know that one. I know it word for word. I just never..."
"Never thought it was yours."

I sit very still on the path. "So the slip's slack was on my docket. And somebody had tied a catch on it, before I ever got there. Waiting. When it let go, the catch made the slack into a nurse and a defibrillator and an ambulance at the lights, and it rode on my docket. So my name rode."
"That's called a snare," says Orla.
"Who could—"
"Lesson's over." She hands me a length of bare cord. "Work that till your hands stop shaking."
They don't stop. I go home after dark, and Dad has left the hall light on for me.
Next morning Mr Pargeter is at my window table in Dorrie's, with a pot of tea for two and a bun cut exactly in half. The hospital band is gone from his wrist. His cardigan is buttoned right.
"Ah," he says. "The clerk. Or rather, the—"
"Still the clerk."
"—the gardener's apprentice, I was going to say." He pours. "Orla tells me you've signed your name to something in her garden."
"She told you? She doesn't discuss her neighbours."

"I'm not a neighbour. I'm a nuisance." He waits while the nine o'clock bell rings across the road, all nine strokes, as if it would be rude to talk over it. "So. Fair's fair. You've signed yours. I'll sign mine. Pargeter tunes pianos. He's a decent man and I've been him for thirty years. My name is Oake. Cuthbert Oake."
I listen for the humming, the way I listened when he told me 'not the faintest'. There isn't any. There's rain on the window and the last stroke of the bell going away down Tallow Row.
"Why are you telling me?"
"Because I want it back," he says. "And you're a clerk. Clerks find things that have been put away." He slides half the bun across to me. "Go and ask your Archive what it did with me."
I'm suspended. I can't go upstairs. But I cross the road anyway, and Stan puts down his paper.
"You can't go up, Ila."
"I know, Stan."
"But a suspended officer can put in for papers touching her own review." He pushes a request slip across the desk. "That's the rule."
So I write: Staff record, Oake, Cuthbert. Reason: touches my pending case. Which is true, every word, and my heart is going like a tram bell while Stan reads it over.
Twenty minutes later Stan comes down with a buff record card, typed and old.
OAKE, Cuthbert. Knotter, Second Class. Deceased. And under remarks, in careful ink: Corn Exchange collapse. Line of duty. The date is thirty years gone.
I turn and look through the glass doors, and my hands go cold. Across the road, in Dorrie's window, Mr Pargeter is pouring himself more tea. The Bureau buried him thirty years ago.

Orla is weeding when I get to Nettlecombe that afternoon. I put the record card on the potting bench beside the coin, which is still on its edge, and stand there until she looks at it. She does, for a long moment. Then she goes back to the weeds.
"The Bureau says he's been dead thirty years," I say. "The Corn Exchange. And yesterday you told me somebody tied a snare and waited, all that time, for a knot to come undone."
"I told you what a snare is."

"Bureau doctrine says nobody can shape slack. Nobody. Not a Master, not anyone in that building, not anyone who's ever been in it." I can hear my voice going up, the way it does when I'm sure of something. "So who in the world could?"
Orla doesn't stop weeding. She works a dandelion loose, root and all, and drops it in her bucket.
"I did," she says. "Thirty years ago."
